lesson.arabic-quranic-scope.title_en: Three kinds of study: اللُّغَة, التَّفْسِير, التَّجْوِيد
lesson.arabic-quranic-scope.family_en: Keeping language study apart from commentary and from recitation
steps: Three different things can be studied in a Qur'anic text: its language, its التَّفْسِير, commentary, and its التَّجْوِيد, the rules for reciting it. This module is about the first.
A grammar point explains how the words relate. Commentary is a separate discipline, with its own sources and teachers.
A translation is one reading of the meaning, so it's often called تَرْجَمَةُ الْمَعَانِي, a translation of the meanings.
Recitation is learnt by ear, from a qualified teacher or a trusted recording.

examples.en: I'm studying the text's language, not its commentary.
This is a translation of the meanings.
I learnt the rules of recitation with a teacher.

why.q_en: Why is a translation called تَرْجَمَةُ الْمَعَانِي, a translation of the meanings?
why.a_en: Because any translation is one reading of the meaning, put into other words. The Arabic text stays the text; a translation is a guide to it.

selftest.why_en: It's learnt by ear, with a teacher.
A separate discipline, with its own sources.

quotes.en: Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds.
quotes.note_en: A language note: الْحَمْدُ ends in -u, the nominative: it's the subject of a sentence without a verb, and the next word says to whom it belongs. What the verse means more fully is a question for commentary.

leads_to.en: The muṣḥaf's own spelling, and how it differs from modern spelling.

lesson.arabic-uthmani-script.title_en: The muṣḥaf's spelling: الرَّسْم and الضَّبْط
lesson.arabic-uthmani-script.family_en: How the muṣḥaf's spelling differs from modern spelling, and why a quote keeps it

table.en: a small alif, written above a letter

steps: Printed muṣḥafs keep an old الرَّسْم, spelling, with their own الضَّبْط, marks and signs, so many words look different from modern Arabic.
A small alif above a letter stands for a long ā that modern spelling writes in full. In the first quote, the last word is الْعَالَمِينَ in modern spelling.
An alif with a small sign on top marks هَمْزَةُ الْوَصْلِ, the joining hamza, which is silent when words run together.
Some words keep an older spelling: الصَّلَاة is written with a و in the muṣḥaf, as the second quote shows.
Pause signs and other marks belong to the muṣḥaf's own system: look them up in its guide. Quote the muṣḥaf exactly, and write your own notes in modern spelling.

examples.en: The muṣḥaf is written in the Uthmani spelling.

examples.ar: لِكُلِّ عَلَامَةٍ مَعْنًى فِي دَلِيلِ الرُّمُوزِ.
examples.en: Each sign has a meaning in the guide to the symbols.

why.q_en: Why not modernise the muṣḥaf's spelling when you quote it?
why.a_en: The spelling is part of the text as it has been handed down, and each sign has a meaning in its edition's guide. Quote it exactly, name the edition, and keep your own writing in modern spelling.

selftest.why_en: From رَسَمَ, to draw: the letters as drawn, before anything is added to them.

selftest.q_en: In the muṣḥaf, what does a small alif above a letter stand for?
selftest.why_en: Modern spelling writes that ā in full.
The letters themselves are the رَسْم.

quotes.en: Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds.
quotes.note_en: In modern spelling, the last word is الْعَالَمِينَ, with its long ā written in full.

quotes.en: and they keep up the prayer
quotes.note_en: In modern spelling, the second word is الصَّلَاةَ, with an alif for its long ā.

leads_to.en: Taking a word apart with a morphology annotation.

lesson.arabic-quranic-morphology.title_en: Morphology as an aid: prefix, stem and suffix
lesson.arabic-quranic-morphology.family_en: Reading a morphology annotation: the parts of a written word, and what each tells you
steps: A morphology annotation splits a written word into its parts, and labels each one: person, number, case or mood.

In the quote's وَإِيَّاكَ, an annotation shows two parts: وَ, and; and إِيَّاكَ, you, the object pronoun that stands before its verb. Grammarians take it further, into إِيَّا and كَ, the part that says who.
نَسْتَعِينُ, we seek help, is a form X verb from ع-و-ن, help, with نَـ, we, as its prefix: the pattern اِسْتَفْعَلَ often means seeking something.
Read the tag definitions rather than guessing at abbreviations, and note anything you can't explain, to check later.

examples.ar: تَتَكَوَّنُ الْكَلِمَةُ مِنْ سَابِقَةٍ وَجِذْعٍ وَلَاحِقَةٍ.
examples.en: The word is made up of a prefix, a stem and a suffix.
Yūsuf asked his friend for help.

why.q_en: Why does an annotation split وَإِيَّاكَ at all?
why.a_en: The وَ links it to what comes before, and إِيَّاكَ is a word of its own: the object pronoun used when the object stands before its verb. One dictionary entry wouldn't show that.

selftest.q_en: In نَسْتَعِينُ, what does نَـ tell you?
selftest.why_en: It's the prefix of a present verb for "we".

selftest.q_en: What does the pattern اِسْتَفْعَلَ often add?
selftest.why_en: Form X, as in seeking help.

quotes.en: You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.
quotes.note_en: A language note: إِيَّاكَ, you, comes before its verb, and نَسْتَعِينُ is form X of ع-و-ن.

leads_to.en: Reading a word inside its clause and its passage.

lesson.arabic-quranic-context.title_en: Meaning in context: the pronoun, the particle, the passage
lesson.arabic-quranic-context.family_en: Reading a word inside its clause and passage, and comparing translations
steps: Read a word inside its clause and its passage before you draw anything wider from it.
Find what each pronoun refers to: in the quote, the كَ of رَبِّكَ, your Lord, refers to the one addressed, and الَّذِي, who, refers back to رَبّ.
Compare two translations: where their wording differs, look at the Arabic relationship first, then name the difference as a translator's choice.
A grammatical possibility isn't automatically the intended meaning: for questions of interpretation, go to qualified commentary.

examples.en: The two translations differed over one word.
The meaning becomes clear from the context.

examples.ar: رَجَعْتُ إِلَى التَّفْسِيرِ فِي هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةِ.
examples.en: I turned to the commentary on this question.

why.q_en: Why compare translations, rather than pick one?
why.a_en: Each translator makes choices the English needs, and one English word can't carry every shade of the Arabic. Comparing them shows where the choices lie, and the Arabic shows what they're choosing between.

selftest.why_en: The clause and the passage around a word.

selftest.q_en: In رَبِّكَ, who does كَ refer to?
Two translations word a phrase differently. What do you look at first?
selftest.why_en: Then name the difference as a translator's choice.

quotes.en: Read in the name of your Lord who created.
quotes.note_en: A language note: اِقْرَأْ is a command to one person, and the pronoun in رَبِّكَ addresses that person.

leads_to.en: Putting it together in a sourced study of a short passage.

lesson.arabic-quranic-reading-project.title_en: A sourced passage study: الْمُصْحَف, الْمَرَاجِع, حُدُودُ الدِّرَاسَةِ
lesson.arabic-quranic-reading-project.family_en: The words for a study's sources, scope and limits

table.en: a printed copy of the Qur'an

steps: State the study's purpose and its النِّطَاق, its scope: a few verses, studied as language.
Name the مُصْحَف, the printed edition, and the رِوَايَة, the transmission of the reading, it follows, and check every quote against it.
For each word, give its reference, its form and its analysis, with the source of that analysis. Mark your own analysis as yours.
End with حُدُودُ الدِّرَاسَةِ, the study's limits, and any مَسْأَلَةٌ مَفْتُوحَةٌ, open question: what the study doesn't settle.

examples.ar: اِعْتَمَدْتُ عَلَى طَبْعَةٍ مَعْرُوفَةٍ مِنَ الْمُصْحَفِ.
examples.en: I relied on a well-known printed edition of the Qur'an.
I named the source of each analysis.

why.q_en: Why name the edition and the reading?
why.a_en: Printed copies follow a transmitted reading, and editions can differ in their signs. Naming them lets someone else check every quote against the same text.

choices: a printed copy of the Qur'an
selftest.answer: a printed copy of the Qur'an
selftest.why_en: The text is quoted from one, by edition.
What the study covers, and so what it leaves out.

selftest.q_en: What goes with each word you analyse?
choices: its reference, and the source of the analysis
selftest.answer: its reference, and the source of the analysis
selftest.why_en: So someone else can check it.
